meta.title: Who really said "Vision is the art of seeing what is invisible to others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jonathan Swift wrote the thought — but as "Vision is the art of seeing things invisible." The popular "…to others" wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Vision is the art of seeing what is invisible to others'?
meta.ogDescription: Swift's real line is "Vision is the art of seeing things invisible" from Thoughts on Various Subjects. The "…to others" version is a modern rewording.

answer.label: Not quite Swift’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Swift’s, but he wrote it more tersely: “Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible,” a stand-alone aphorism in his Thoughts on Various Subjects. The circulating “…seeing what is invisible to others” is a later expansion that appears in none of his works — a paraphrase dressed up as a quotation.

source.excerpt: Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible.
trail: Swift’s genuine text reads “Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible” in the Wikisource text of Thoughts on Various Subjects ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists only the short form under its sourced Thoughts on Various Subjects section; the “to others” variant is absent.
Quote aggregators such as Quotefancy ↗ circulate the expanded “…what is invisible to others” wording with no source citation.
Goodreads ↗ preserves the correct short form, showing both versions travel side by side.
source.excerptNote: Swift’s actual aphorism — note there is no “to others.” The four extra words are a later addition.

source.rightsNote: Swift’s Thoughts on Various Subjects was first collected in the early 1700s and is long in the public domain. The expanded “…to others” wording has no identifiable modern author and is a trivial restatement of Swift’s public-domain line, so nothing here is under copyright.

author.name: Jonathan Swift
author.heading: About Jonathan Swift
author.metaLine: 1667–1745 · Anglo-Irish satirist, essayist & Dean of St Patrick's
author.bio: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish satirist and clergyman, author of Gulliver’s Travels (1726) and A Modest Proposal (1729). Alongside his major satires he kept collections of aphorisms — most notably Thoughts on Various Subjects — compact maxims prized for their wit, which is why single lines from them circulate so widely today.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake attribution — it is a genuine Swift thought that has been quietly reworded. The result is a “quotation” that sounds like Swift but is not what he wrote.

items.why: Swift wrote “Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible” — four words shorter and with no “to others.” The expanded form appears in none of his texts; the primary text ↗ and the Wikiquote sourced section ↗ both carry only the short form.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Swift’s; the exact sentence is not. His real line is “Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible,” per Thoughts on Various Subjects ↗.

context.heading: Why the wording drifted
lead: Swift’s original is an epigram: “Vision is the Art of seeing Things invisible.” Its power is its compression. The modern “…seeing what is invisible to others” recasts the line as a leadership maxim — vision as the founder’s edge — which is why it thrives in business and motivational settings even though Swift never framed it that way.
Both versions now circulate together, but only the short one is his. It is a textbook case of a real quotation being ‘improved’ until it stops being a quotation.
